paragraphs: The remaining charge against the House of Representatives that I am to examine rests on a supposition that the number of members will not be increased from time to time as the growth of population may require.

It has been admitted that this objection, if well supported, would carry great weight. The following observations will show that, like most other objections against the Constitution, it can come only from an incomplete view of the subject, or from a jealousy that discolors and distorts every object it looks at.

1. Those who press the objection seem not to have remembered that the federal Constitution does not suffer by comparison with the State constitutions in the security it provides for a gradual increase in the number of representatives. The number that is to apply at first is declared to be temporary, and its duration is limited to the short term of three years.

Within every successive term of ten years a census of the inhabitants is to be repeated. The unmistakable objects of these regulations are, first, to readjust from time to time the apportionment of representatives to the number of inhabitants, with the single exception that each State shall have at least one representative; and second, to increase the number of representatives at the same intervals, with the sole limit that the whole number shall not exceed one for every thirty thousand inhabitants. If we review the constitutions of the individual States, we shall find that some of them contain no definite regulations on this subject, that others correspond pretty much with the federal Constitution on this point, and that the most effective security in any of them comes down to a mere directory provision.

2. So far as experience bears on this subject, the gradual increase of representatives under the State constitutions has at least kept pace with the increase of their constituents, and it appears that the representatives have been as ready to agree to such measures as the constituents have been to ask for them.

3. There is a peculiarity in the federal Constitution that ensures a watchful attention, in a majority both of the people and of their representatives, to a constitutional increase in the number of the latter. The peculiarity is that one branch of the legislature represents citizens and the other represents the States. In the former, consequently, the larger States will have the most weight; in the latter, the advantage will lie with the smaller States. From this we may infer with certainty that the larger States will be strenuous advocates for increasing the number and weight of that part of the legislature in which their influence predominates. And it so happens that four of the largest States alone will have a majority of all the votes in the House of Representatives. Should the representatives or the people of the smaller States ever oppose a reasonable addition of members, a coalition of a very few States will be enough to overrule the opposition. Such a coalition might be prevented on ordinary occasions by rivalry and local prejudices, but it would not fail to form when it was prompted not merely by common interest but also justified by equity and the principles of the Constitution.

It may perhaps be alleged that the Senate would be prompted by like motives to an opposing coalition, and that, since its concurrence would be indispensable, the just and constitutional views of the other branch might be defeated. This is the difficulty that has probably caused the most serious apprehensions among the jealous friends of a numerous representation. Fortunately it is one of those difficulties that exist only in appearance and vanish on close and accurate inspection. If I am not mistaken, the following reflections will be admitted to be conclusive and satisfactory on this point.

Although the two houses will have equal authority on all legislative subjects except the originating of money bills, it cannot be doubted that the House, being composed of the greater number of members, when supported by the more powerful States and speaking the known and settled view of a majority of the people, will have no small advantage in any question that depends on the relative firmness of the two houses.

This advantage must be increased by the consciousness on the one side of being supported in its demands by right, by reason and by the Constitution, and by the consciousness on the opposite side of contending against the force of all these solemn considerations.

It must be considered further that in the gradation between the smallest and the largest States there are several that, though in general most likely to arrange themselves among the former, are too little removed in size and population from the latter to support an opposition to the latter's just and legitimate claims. Hence it is by no means certain that a majority of votes, even in the Senate, would be unfriendly to proper increases in the number of representatives.

It will not be looking too far ahead to add that the senators from all the new States may be won over to the just views of the House of Representatives by an expedient too obvious to be overlooked. As these States will for a great length of time grow in population with peculiar rapidity, they will be interested in frequent reapportionments of the representatives to the number of inhabitants. The large States, therefore, which will prevail in the House of Representatives, will have nothing to do but make reapportionments and increases conditions of each other. The senators from all the fastest-growing States will then be bound to fight for the increases by the interest their States will feel in the reapportionments.

These considerations seem to afford ample security on this subject, and ought by themselves to satisfy all the doubts and fears that have been indulged about it. Admitting, however, that they should all prove insufficient to overcome the unjust policy of the smaller States, or their predominant influence in the councils of the Senate, the larger States still have a constitutional and infallible resource by which they will be able at all times to accomplish their just purposes. The House of Representatives can not only refuse, but alone can propose, the supplies required for the support of government. In a word, they hold the purse. By that powerful instrument, as we see in the history of the British Constitution, an infant and humble representation of the people gradually enlarged the sphere of its activity and importance, and finally reduced, as far as it seems to have wished, all the overgrown prerogatives of the other branches of the government. This power over the purse may in fact be regarded as the most complete and effective weapon with which any constitution can arm the immediate representatives of the people, to obtain redress of every grievance and to carry into effect every just and beneficial measure.

But will not the House of Representatives be as much interested as the Senate in keeping the government in its proper functions, and will it not therefore be unwilling to stake the government's existence or reputation on the Senate's yielding? Or, if such a trial of firmness between the two branches were risked, would not the one be as likely to yield first as the other? These questions will cause no difficulty for those who reflect that in all cases, the smaller the number and the more permanent and conspicuous the position of the men in power, the stronger the interest each of them will individually feel in whatever concerns the government. Those who represent the dignity of their country in the eyes of other nations will be particularly aware of every prospect of public danger or of dishonorable stagnation in public affairs. To these causes we are to ascribe the continual triumph of the British House of Commons over the other branches of the government whenever the engine of a money bill has been used. Absolute inflexibility on the part of the other branches, although it could not have failed to involve every department of the state in general confusion, has neither been feared nor experienced. The utmost firmness that the federal Senate or President can show will not be more than equal to a resistance in which they will be supported by constitutional and patriotic principles.

In this review of the make-up of the House of Representatives, I have passed over the considerations of economy which, in the present state of affairs, might have had some effect in reducing the temporary number of representatives. Disregarding them would probably have given as rich a theme for denunciation of the Constitution as the smallness of the proposed number has done. I also omit any remarks on the difficulty that might be found, under present circumstances, in engaging in the federal service a large number of the kind of characters the people will probably elect. One observation, however, I must be permitted to add on this subject, as it claims, in my judgment, very serious attention. It is that in all legislative assemblies, the greater the number of members, the fewer will be the men who in fact direct their proceedings. In the first place, the more numerous an assembly is, of whatever characters it is composed, the greater, as is well known, is the ascendancy of passion over reason. In the next place, the larger the number, the greater the proportion of members of limited information and weak capacities. Now it is precisely on characters of this description that the eloquence and skill of the few are known to act with all their force. In the ancient republics, where the whole body of the people assembled in person, a single orator or an artful statesman was generally seen to rule with as complete a sway as if a scepter had been placed in his single hand. On the same principle, the more numerous a representative assembly is made, the more it will share the weaknesses that belong to collective meetings of the people. Ignorance will be the dupe of cunning, and passion the slave of sophistry and declamation. The people can never err more than in supposing that by multiplying their representatives beyond a certain limit they strengthen the barrier against the government of a few. Experience will forever warn them that, on the contrary, AFTER SECURING A SUFFICIENT NUMBER FOR THE PURPOSES OF SAFETY, OF LOCAL INFORMATION, AND OF DIFFUSIVE SYMPATHY WITH THE WHOLE SOCIETY, they will work against their own aims with every addition to their representatives. The face of the government may become more democratic, but the soul that animates it will be more oligarchic. The machine will be enlarged, but the springs that direct its motions will be fewer, and often more secret.

Connected with the objection about the number of representatives, and properly noticed here, is one that has been raised against the number made competent to conduct legislative business. It has been said that more than a majority ought to have been required for a quorum, and in particular cases, if not in all, more than a majority of a quorum for a decision. It cannot be denied that some advantages might have resulted from such a precaution. It might have been an additional shield for some particular interests, and another general obstacle to hasty and biased measures. But these considerations are outweighed by the drawbacks on the opposite side. In all cases where justice or the general good might require new laws to be passed or active measures to be pursued, the fundamental principle of free government would be reversed. It would no longer be the majority that ruled; the power would be transferred to the minority. If this defensive privilege were limited to particular cases, a self-interested minority might use it to shield themselves from fair sacrifices for the general welfare or, in particular emergencies, to extort unreasonable concessions. Lastly, it would encourage and foster the harmful practice of secessions. This practice has shown itself even in States where only a majority is required. It is a practice destructive of all the principles of order and regular government, and it leads more directly to public convulsions and the ruin of popular governments than any other that has yet been displayed among us.
